extracted.intended_audience: general public and media professionals (readers interested in journalism and media industry news)
extracted.subtask_description: A news transcript reporting the resignation of The New York Times editorial page editor after backlash over a controversial op-ed; explains newsroom reaction, newsroom/editorial separation, policies, and leadership response. The page is aimed at informing readers about the media-industry controversy and its implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publicly trash your own news organization for editorial choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The New York Times has policies, as do many major journalistic outlets, that say, basically, don't trash your own news organization for the editorial choices they make publicly. You're not supposed to do that on social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transcript notes that in the 24–48 hours after the op-ed was posted, many reporters posted reactions on Twitter and other platforms; the policy exists to discourage such public internal criticism even when staff disagree with editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain separation between newsroom reporting and editorial pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms and editorial pages operate separately with separate leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece stresses that when those lines are blurred it creates conflict — reporters felt the op-ed did not represent their journalistic values and said 'this is my brand, my New York Times,' showing how blurring can make editorial decisions feel like newsroom decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial pages should expose readers to a wide range of thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: Veteran journalists argued that editorial pages are supposed to expose readers (and journalists) to a wide range of thoughts and thinking on topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale was offered in defense of publishing controversial viewpoints; it is presented as a guiding principle for why newspapers might invite or run provocative opinion pieces, though the transcript also documents tensions arising from that principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider potential harm and civil-liberties implications when publishing op-eds
rubrics_metrics.description: Times journalists argued the op-ed advocated an extra-legal application of order at the risk of people's rights and could escalate risks to citizens and journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transcript cites concerns about police violating civil liberties and journalists being hurt; editors should weigh whether an opinion piece's advocacy could meaningfully endanger rights or safety when deciding to publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh newsroom morale, representation, and racial-justice considerations in editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Leadership needed to show the newsroom that he heard it, particularly on issues of race and racial justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publisher's and editor's reputations and ability to lead depend on demonstrating responsiveness to newsroom concerns, especially on sensitive topics; failing to do so can undermine trust within the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure editorial decisions are tenable given newsroom support and institutional stability
rubrics_metrics.description: What changed was that the decision to run the piece 'wasn't tenable within the newsroom' — the leadership realized they'd lost the newsroom over this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an op-ed can be defended on principle, editors must consider whether the decision is sustainable given staff backlash and institutional consequences; losing newsroom support can make an editorial stance impractical to maintain.
